title: Serving product-market-fit hypothesis and core narrative
content:
Synopsis:
Redwood helps engineering teams ship dependable LLM features by making inference predictable, affordable, and easy to operate across hosted, reserved, and private environments. This brief reframes our core product-market-fit hypothesis: customers don’t primarily buy models — they buy predictable serving outcomes (latency, cost, reliability, and deployment choice).

Why this matters now:
- Market saturation of accessible models has reduced differentiation by model alone.
- Applications are judged by user experience and unit economics, not model provenance.
- Customers face a fragmented set of choices (managed endpoints, self-hosted runtimes, cloud GPUs) with unclear tradeoffs and heavy ops burden.

Problem statement (customer POV):
- Product and platform teams spend weeks or months tuning infrastructure to meet latency and cost targets.
- Sudden model upgrades or traffic spikes break SLAs or double costs.
- Security teams demand private deployment options but lack a consistent control plane.
- Observability is poor: teams cannot attribute cost to features or identify regressions quickly.

Redwood hypothesis (one-liner):
Teams choose Redwood when they want one predictable serving abstraction that reduces operational load, makes economics visible and actionable, and leaves deployment choices (hosted, dedicated, private) under the customer’s control.

How we win (core advantages):
1) Serving-first economics: we treat token cost, latency, and throughput as first-class product levers. Customers see how batching, caching, and quantization change unit economics in their workload, not in synthetic benchmarks.
2) Consistent developer contract: same API and rollout primitives across hosted/dedicated/private removes engineering friction and rework when customers change deployment modes.
3) Operational safeguards: routing policies, automatic fallbacks, canaries and rollback controls that keep apps online during model or infra churn.
4) Transparent evidence: real customer traces, per-route cost breakdown, and quality monitoring tied to prompt sets so teams can make informed tradeoffs.

Proof points to surface early:
- Benchmarks that show 20–50% lower per-token cost on representative SaaS workloads when using default optimizer settings.
- Case study: marketplace search provider cut 95th percentile latency by 30ms after switching to Redwood routing + KV caching.
- Compliance-ready private deployment with KMS/HSM integrations validated in a regulated pilot.

Three illustrative customer scenarios (micro-stories):
1) Growth-stage chat app: wants predictable monthly bill and no regressions after upgrading to a new model. Redwood: canary deploys + auto-fallback to legacy model and per-feature cost attribution.
2) Enterprise contact center: must keep audio-to-text and summarization in a private VPC. Redwood: private control plane + local inference that matches hosted APIs for developer speed.
3) Platform team at large consumer app: needs routing policies to trade latency for cost at peak. Redwood: region-aware routing with capacity-aware fallbacks and SLO-safe batching.

Competitive posture (short):
- Managed-model APIs: simple but opaque economics and fewer deployment options.
- Self-hosted runtimes: maximum control but high ops burden and slow developer velocity.
- Cloud GPU endpoints/marketplaces: flexible hardware but inconsistent inference feature set and limited rollouts/observability.
Redwood sits between managed simplicity and self-hosted control: opinionated tooling to reduce ops and maximize predictable economics.

Core messaging pillars (3):
A) Predictable Serving Outcomes — "Measureable economics and latency under your workload."
B) Unified Developer Surface — "One API. Same rollout controls. Any deployment."
C) Production Reliability — "Graceful fallbacks and operational guardrails that keep features online."

Top objections and suggested rebuttals:
- "We can just run models ourselves." -> Rebuttal: If you can, great — Redwood’s dedicated/private modes integrate with that flow and add rollout/observability primitives that teams rarely build well.
- "Proprietary models are the moat." -> Rebuttal: Models are a moat for research; serving consistency and measurable economics are the moat for product delivery and adoption.
- "This looks expensive." -> Rebuttal: Show per-route cost breakdowns and simulated savings from batching/caching; highlight predictable unit economics versus surprise bills.

Early GTM experiments to validate narrative:
- Run a 6-week pilot program with 3 customers: ecommerce search, chat startup, healthcare enterprise. Capture before/after P95 latency and per-feature token cost.
- Publish two short technical case studies with concrete numbers and configuration recipes.
- Create a short interactive landing page where visitors can upload a prompt profile and get an estimated cost/latency improvement using Redwood optimizations.

Messaging dos/don’ts for sales collateral:
- Do: lead with outcomes (latency, cost, reliability) and show specific numbers or ranges.
- Do: highlight deployment flexibility early for security-conscious buyers.
- Don’t: bury the ops story in product jargon — platform and infra buyers care about processes and guardrails.

Asks and next steps:
- Align on 2 canonical benchmark workloads to include in sales collateral (chat, retrieval-augmented search).
- Product: ship a simplified per-route savings report in the console by Q1.
- GTM: commit to three pilot customers for the 6-week validation.

Appendix (notes for comms):
- Avoid claiming "absolute lowest cost" — prefer "lowered unit cost in realistic workloads" and show how it varies by workload.
- Keep the narrative focused on "serving outcomes" rather than model selection.

Owner notes:
Drafted to center GTM experiments and create a testable PMF hypothesis. Feedback welcome from product marketing, solutions engineering, and applied ML on the benchmark choices and the pilot qualification criteria.
